We prove that this bound is sharp, that is, $χ(L_{D_n})=2n+2$.

papers.title: Properties of the Dichromatic Polynomial
papers.abstract: The chromatic polynomial is a well-studied function of graphs whose coefficients, factorization, and other properties are well-known to encode structural information about the underlying graph. An analogous notion of graph colouring exists for directed graphs which is also well-studied, but little is yet known about the corresponding dichromatic polynomial. We investigate properties of the dichromatic polynomial, including its coefficient interpretations, root-dense regions, and asymptotic growth. We also show that chordal digraphs' polynomials split into linear factors in a way analogous to the undirected case, confirm a conjecture on dichromatic uniqueness posed by González-Moreno et al., and study the density of dichromatic polynomials within certain larger families of polynomials.

papers.title: Heterogeneous and episodic permeability evolution and correlation with acoustic emission activity during faulting in granite
papers.abstract: Rock permeability changes dramatically during brittle deformation, affecting faulting dynamics and crustal fluid flow. Here, we combine fluid-flow and local pore-pressure measurements acquired during a quasi-static shear-failure test in Westerly granite with a three-dimensional finite-element inverse method. The measured flow rate and six internal pore pressures constrain the local hydraulic transmissivities (permeability-thickness products) of ten cells along the growing fault. Synthetic ensembles anchored to the pressure-sensor accuracy recover these transmissivities with median mean errors of 7-9%, with the fault ends generally better resolved than the interior. Applied to the experiment, the method resolves episodic transmissivity increases, interspersed with decreases, through fault growth and slip. Local values reach approximately $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ m$^3$ (16 times the bulk contribution), and the final-stage values vary by a factor of 2.3 along the fault. Across cells, the median absolute change in recovered transmissivity is at most about 16% for $\pm50\%$ changes in assumed fault-zone thickness. The local one-dimensional estimates of Aben et al. (2024) agree in scale with the three-dimensional results, with a median 3-D/apparent ratio of 0.81. Cumulative acoustic-emission counts track the overall hydraulic evolution, but the relations of local event density, its stagewise increments and amplitude-weighted activity to transmissivity vary between cells. The comparison distinguishes the value of AE for mapping damage growth from quantitative hydraulic prediction using event-count and relative-amplitude metrics.

papers.title: RaMOD: Moving-Object Detection from Raw mmWave Radar Cubes under Ego Motion
papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides weather-robust sensing and direct Doppler measurements, yet automotive perception pipelines often reduce its output to sparse point clouds or two-dimensional projections, leaving raw range-azimuth-Doppler (RAD) cubes underutilized. Ego motion induces Doppler responses from world-static structures, while Doppler wrapping aliases radial velocities, complicating moving-object detection and velocity estimation. We present RaMOD (Radar-based Moving-Object Detection), a real-time framework for moving-object detection and velocity estimation from raw RAD cubes acquired by a vehicle-mounted single-chip radar. RaMOD explicitly estimates frame-wise ego motion and uses the estimated radar translational velocity to predict the Doppler region of world-static structures and suppress returns within it. It temporally encodes the suppressed cubes into multi-scale features to predict RAD-space boxes with class labels. For each detected object, it predicts radial and forward velocities under raw-Doppler and Doppler-unwrapped hypotheses, together with Doppler-wrapping probabilities. On our BRIDGE-Liv dataset, RaMOD outperforms all compared raw-radar methods across RAD-cube, RA, and RD detection settings, achieving 80.8% cube mAP at IoU 0.30, 15.7 percentage points above the strongest RAD-cube baseline. Velocity MAE is 1.128 m/s, with 99.87% Doppler-wrapping accuracy.

papers.title: What drives the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in large language models?
papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.

papers.title: Viscosity heats, diffusion drains: Open-system thermodynamics in unimodular cosmology
papers.abstract: In GR with bulk viscosity and in unimodular gravity with energy diffusion, the matter sector is non-adiabatic, and their balance, entropy, and temperature equations match if $Π\leftrightarrow \dot{Q}/3H$. Disagreement over whether unimodular cosmology is adiabatic comes from assigning entropy to matter only or to the total effective fluid. The key is the temperature $T_D$ of the sector absorbing the diffused energy: comoving entropy production is $\dot{Q}(1/T_D-1/T_m)$, yielding earlier limits for $T_D \rightarrow \infty$ and $T_D \rightarrow T_m$. For finite $T_D$, diffusion acts like heat exchange with an external reservoir: unlike viscosity, which only heats a closed fluid, diffusion into a colder bath can cool an open one, breaking the viscosity-diffusion correspondence for observables and stability. Cosmographically, $Π$ is fixed by the deceleration $q$, while diffusion is fixed by the jerk $j$; thus $Λ$CDM is the adiabatic limit of unimodular cosmology but remains dissipative when modeled via viscosity. The diffusive analogue of $|Π|/ρ$ is the shift $c_s^2-ω$ in effective sound speed, set by perturbative stability rather than acceleration. If dark matter is a gas with conserved rest mass, consistent diffusion removes only thermal energy, forbids phantom behavior, and bounds the growth of the cosmological term by the finite thermal reservoir; producing a logotropic dark fluid with conserved particle number would require relativistic dark matter at $z\simeq12$. With the Hayward-Kodama apparent-horizon temperature, the generalized second law in unimodular gravity follows from the local one, whereas for bulk viscosity it must be imposed separately.

papers.title: Force-Closure Condition for Cooperative Multi-robot Pushing of Rectangular Objects
papers.abstract: In cooperative object manipulation, the placement of pushing contacts determines whether force closure can be achieved and agents can generate arbitrary forces and torques on the object correspondingly. This study derives a necessary and sufficient closed-form condition for the planar force closure of a rectangular object, a common object shape in everyday settings, under four frictionless pushing contacts. For a rectangle of length $b$ and width $a$, force closure holds if and only if $(l_1+l_3-b)(l_2+l_4-a)<0$, where $l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4$ are the four edge contact locations. This condition is independent of the object's center of mass and is used to verify contact configurations before contact force allocation. When the condition is not satisfied, the signs of the two factors indicate which opposing contact pair should be adjusted. The condition and adjustment rule are then integrated into a full-pose trajectory-tracking framework as a geometric feasibility layer to demonstrate their use in control. Static wrench feasibility tests validate the proposed condition, while narrow-passage floating-body simulations show that maintaining a force-closure configuration reduces the RMS tracking errors in $x$, $y$, and unwrapped yaw from $12.05$ m, $18.11$ m, and $535.96^\circ$ to $2.24$ m, $2.66$ m, and $2.69^\circ$, respectively.

papers.title: The Cayley-Bedregal reduction for Milnor and Hirzebruch-Milnor classes
papers.abstract: The Cayley--Bedregal reduction replaces a complete intersection $\{f_1=\dots=f_r=0\}$ by the hypersurface $\sum_iφ_if_i=0$ in the projectivized dual bundle. For an isolated complete intersection singularity of corank $c$, we express the Milnor class of this hypersurface on its singular fibre $\mathbb P^{c-1}$ in terms of the Milnor numbers of generic systems obtained by taking linear combinations of the defining equations. Its degree is the original Milnor number, and the higher components recover the Milnor numbers of the systems with fewer equations. These numbers are invariants of the analytic germ. Our second main result concerns the Hodge-theoretic refinement. For a complete intersection defined by a regular section of a rank-$r$ algebraic vector bundle, the Hirzebruch--Milnor class is determined by that of the Cayley--Bedregal hypersurface: the push-forward of the normalized Hirzebruch--Milnor class of the hypersurface, in the sense of Cappell, Maxim, Schürmann and Shaneson, is $(-y)^{r-1}$ times that of the complete intersection, with no positivity assumption on the bundle. The factor $(-y)^{r-1}$ comes from the motivic decomposition of the projective bundle, and at $y=-1$ the identity recovers Aluffi's comparison of Milnor classes. When the tautological bundle is very ample, the hypersurface formula of Maxim, Saito and Schürmann then gives the Hirzebruch--Milnor class of the complete intersection through the vanishing cycles of a single function, avoiding their induction through intermediate complete intersections and their restriction to powers of one line bundle. In integral homology we prove the analytic form of Aluffi's identity, and obtain formulas for the Milnor class in terms of local Milnor fibres and for the Chern--Schwartz--MacPherson class of any projective scheme.

papers.title: Challenging the hoop conjecture with spinning pancakes and baguettes
papers.abstract: Understanding when gravitational collapse produces a black hole remains a central challenge in general relativity. Black-hole uniqueness results characterize the stationary endpoint under suitable assumptions, while singularity theorems establish geodesic incompleteness in the presence of trapped surfaces and appropriate energy and global conditions. Neither, however, provides a general criterion for horizon formation. The hoop conjecture offers such a criterion by relating the enclosed mass to the compactness of a matter distribution in every direction. We construct axisymmetric families of initial data describing rotating dust and test a formulation of the conjecture adapted to this setting. We explore highly prolate and oblate configurations with both constant and differential rescaled angular-velocity profiles, including configurations near the threshold for apparent-horizon formation. We find that the conjecture holds for rotating configurations, with a coefficient within 14% of unity as in the nonrotating case, provided the quasilocal mass includes the rotational energy. If the irreducible mass of the apparent horizon is used instead, the deviations grow with spin, as they do for Kerr black holes. For horizonless configurations, the conjecture likewise holds when the mass is restricted to the energy enclosed by the matter surface, whereas using the ADM mass, which also includes rotational field energy outside the matter, leads to apparent violations of up to $\approx$25%. We also discuss the possible evolution of compact configurations without apparent horizons, their relation to weak cosmic censorship, and their implications for horizonless compact objects.

papers.title: Effect of car-centric social norms on traffic congestion in a compartmental model of transit mode utilization
papers.abstract: Vehicle traffic congestion is a persistent feature of urban transportation systems around the world.Importantly, congestion is in part a consequence of human decision-making: car traffic is reduced when people choose modes of transportation such as metro trains, buses, or trams, over cars, and it is amplified when there is a persistent social bias towards driving. The underlying feedback loop in which traffic levels influence transportation mode choices, which in turn affect traffic levels themselves, is poorly understood and we study its consequences in the presented work using a compartmental modeling approach. We first consider a simplified model of only car traffic and show that it predicts a hysteresis between congested and uncongested states, which is consistent with broader literature on on traffic modeling. Next, we add buses and trains to the model as alternative transit modes, confirm the existence of hysteresis in this generalization, and derive the relative trip completion rates of each mode. Finally, to account for decision-making, we take the demand rates for the different transit modes to be dynamic, closing the feedback loop between mode choice and utilization. This redistributes demand for each mode of transportation, highlighting that traffic conditions may be a key aspect of mode choice. Furthermore, our model predicts that increasing public awareness of congestion can be an effective control strategy to increase utilization of public transit. However, car-centric social norms must be sufficiently small, or car use is instead amplified.

papers.title: Hybridization-brightened interlayer excitons in multilayer WSe2 controlled by sliding ferroelectricity
papers.abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) combine spatially separated electron and hole wavefunctions with electrically tunable dipole moments, but their reduced wavefunction overlap generally limits optical emission, particularly for high-energy states. Here we report a bright, spectrally narrow high-energy interlayer exciton (h-IX) near 2.23 eV in few-layer WSe2 and investigate how its optical activity evolves with layer number and sliding-ferroelectric polarization. In pristine 2H-WSe2, we observe thickness-dependent brightening of high-energy exciton emission. GW-BSE calculations reveal mixed intralayer and interlayer configurations with enhanced optical weight, suggesting that multilayer hybridization contributes to the observed brightening. In parallel-stacked 3L/3L WSe2 containing a sliding-ferroelectric interface, the h-IX exhibits polarization-dependent energies and Stark responses that distinguish Pup and Pdown domains. Electric-field-driven domain-wall motion produces hysteretic transfer of spectral weight between the two h-IX branches, enabling optical tracking of ferroelectric switching. These results establish multilayer hybridization as a route to optically active high-energy interlayer excitons and sliding ferroelectricity as a complementary degree of freedom for controlling their energy, dipole and emission.

papers.title: Global regularity of axisymmetric Navier--Stokes equations under total slip and critical smallness
papers.abstract: We study the axisymmetric incompressible Navier--Stokes equations in a finite cylinder subject to the Navier--total--slip boundary condition, that is, the Navier slip condition with zero friction. We prove that the solution remains smooth for all time provided that the initial swirl $Γ_0 = r v_{θ,0}$ has zero mean and an explicit smallness condition on the initial data holds. The condition involves $Γ= rv_θ$ and the variables $V = v_θ/\sqrt{r}$ and $Ω= ω_θ/r$, and it is invariant under the natural scaling of the Navier--Stokes equations, hence critical. The total-slip condition produces a boundary term on the lateral wall that cannot be controlled by the dissipation alone; we overcome this with a sharp trace-type identity combined with a remainder controlled by $\|Γ\|_{L^2}$. In addition, the Robin-type boundary condition $\partial_r Γ= 2Γ$ destroys the maximum principle for $Γ$, and we replace it with a uniform $L^4$ bound. These estimates yield uniform $L^4$ bounds for the velocity, and regularity follows from the Ladyzhenskaya--Prodi--Serrin criterion together with boundary regularity results for the Navier slip condition.

papers.title: Adaptive Residual Quantization for Memory-Efficient Temporal Action Segmentation
papers.abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.

papers.title: Expiscating the black hole singularity in holography
papers.abstract: We argue that the leading exponential rate in the high frequency asymptotics of holographic thermal two-point functions is independent of the conformal dimension and spin (held fixed) of the operator. We analyze the leading universal WKB spectral curve governing the asymptotics at non-vanishing momentum scaling with frequency. We show that its classical action governs time domain signatures of the bouncing geodesic singularity, highly damped quasinormal modes, and the asymptotics of multi-stress tensor OPE coefficients. Beyond the leading order, we examine linear and dimension-dependent sublinear scalings of momentum with frequency. In both regimes, we derive the connection matrix between the boundary and the horizon using exact-WKB techniques. The results show a factorization of the spectral function into a perturbative part controlled by the OPE and a non-perturbative part governed by WKB transport. For linear scaling at fixed $k/ω$ in the timelike regime, the turning points controlling physical transport remain separated from the curvature singularity. Nevertheless, a singularity-anchored representative of the same transport homology class determines the leading WKB action. In the sublinear regime, the relevant turning points approach the singularity. We match an exact solution of the near-singularity scaled equation to the exterior WKB solution to determine the connection matrix and spectral function. Our results clarify how the black hole curvature singularity is encoded in dual field theory observables at leading order in the planar expansion.

papers.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
papers.abstract: Atmospheric variability provides a unique window into the three-dimensional structure, dynamics, and evolution of brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. Recent JWST time-resolved spectroscopic observations have revealed complex wavelength-dependent variability, offering unprecedented insights into cloud structures, thermal perturbations, and atmospheric chemistry. However, existing programs have focused primarily on individual benchmarks and specific scientific questions, resulting in heterogeneous spectral and temporal coverage and leaving important regions of the substellar population underexplored, particularly across a broad range of rotation periods, spectral types, and viewing geometries. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could systematically investigate substellar weather across a diverse, well-characterized population. By combining broad infrared spectroscopic coverage with observations spanning multiple rotations and strategically selected epochs, this program would constrain the contributions of different physical mechanisms while investigating how atmospheric structures depend on rotation, viewing geometry, and fundamental physical properties. Extended monitoring would also improve rotational-period determinations and reveal how atmospheric features evolve from rotation to rotation and over longer timescales. This coordinated effort would provide a consistently designed and uniformly processed dataset of time-resolved spectra and variability diagnostics, enabling population-level comparisons, testing predictions from three-dimensional circulation models, and establishing a framework for interpreting the atmospheric diversity and evolution of brown dwarfs and directly imaged giant exoplanets.

papers.title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
papers.abstract: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.

papers.title: Which Acoustic Features Survive Compression? Tracker-Estimated First-Formant Statistics for Codec-Robust Audio DeepfakeDetection
papers.abstract: Audio deepfake detectors that work well on clean lab recordings often degrade after telephone or platform compression. This paper asks a specific question: which low-dimensional acoustic descriptors stay informative after codec degradation? We screen 36 utterance-level features(formants, PNCCs, LFCCs, prosody) on ASVspoof 2019 data and test on the official ASVspoof 2021 LA set across seven codec conditions. Of 33 statistically significant descriptors, only four show large practical separation (|r| >0.5, bootstrap 95% CIs), all first-formant (F1) measures, highly redundant (PC1: 79% variance). The payoff is stability: the 36-feature SVM degrades 14 pp under codec mismatch (9.5%-23.5% EER), while the four-feature RBF-SVM degrades only 5.9 pp (17.0%-22.9%). The F1 subset varies 3.4 pp across conditions versus 13.1 pp for the full set. F1 differences persist after controlling for speaker identity (p greater than 10^10, mixed-effects model). The results suggest that physically interpretable F1 statistics offer a compact, codec-stable diagnostic signal that may complement higher accuracy neural detectors.

papers.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
papers.abstract: Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2-15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 $μ$m. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.

papers.title: Image-Driven Control with Application to Thermoforming
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Image-Driven Control (IDC), an approach to vision-based feedback that operates directly in the image space. IDC offers a direct end-to-end solution in the behavioral framework. Targeting a limited subset of vision-based feedback problems, including applications in manufacturing, the IDC design builds on a computationally advantageous subspace predictive control formulation and offset-free tracking to enable reference tracking in the image space under input and pixel-level constraints. IDC provides a control-theoretic alternative to vision-based feedback systems, enabling improved transparency for analysis and tuning of end-to-end control. It offers straightforward experiment design, an advantage in applications where data collection is expensive. The effectiveness of IDC is shown in a simulation example using a nonlinear high-fidelity model of the heating phase of the thermoforming process.

papers.title: Understanding Coronal `Seeing' using High Angular Resolution Radio Observations of Active Solar Emissions
papers.abstract: Solar radio bursts are generated through the plasma emission mechanism by beams of accelerated electrons travelling along magnetic field lines. They serve as powerful probes of the ambient coronal plasma and magnetic fields. At low frequencies, however, propagation through the turbulent, magnetised coronal plasma strongly modifies their observed properties. Disentangling these propagation effects from the intrinsic nature of the emission therefore remains a major challenge. Despite the long history of observations, there are only a few that leverage high-angular-resolution imaging. This is primarily due to the prevailing expectations that scattering from coronal density inhomogeneities significantly increases the apparent source size, obscuring any fine-scale structures that might be present. While small-scale features are routinely observed in EUV and X-rays, few are detected at meter wavelengths. Numerous studies have focused on quantifying the effect of scattering on the observed apparent size of a point solar radio source. Naturally, their results vary significantly depending on the specifics of the model used to describe coronal inhomogeneities and the scattering prescription applied -- ranging from sub-arcseconds to arcminutes. Recent high angular resolution observations with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) -pathfinders, uGMRT and LOFAR, have revealed unexpectedly compact sources, with sizes as small as $\sim9$ arcseconds in type-I noise storms. Forthcoming high-fidelity and angular resolution SKAO observations will transform our understanding of solar radio emissions by constraining scattering models, improving coronal diagnostics, and revealing fine structures crucial for understanding solar radio emissions and propagation effects.

papers.title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent fails part-way through a long task, the usual analysis records a symptom: a failure-mode label, or the agent and step judged responsible. It does not say where the error entered, which state carried it to the symptom, whether anything in the trajectory contradicted it, or which control could have caught it. We define an episode record that ties a candidate fault to its origin, propagation, detection, response and consequence, located by operational phase and state domain, and that names the control families whose observation and reach cover it. We turned the record into a written annotation protocol and applied it to 95 failed runs of six multi-agent systems from the public Who&When and MAD corpora, reading each trajectory in full. Faults enter early (median at 0.18 of the run), mostly as wrong decisions or fabrications over task state, and in 37 of 88 Who&When runs before the step the corpus' human labels mark as decisive. In 72% of failed runs the trajectory already contained evidence against the error before the failure; in 88% of those no agent acted on it. Something flagged a deviation in 31% of runs, but no response removed the deviated state. Independent judges reading the unused evidence, task contracts fixed at admission, and re-checking beliefs against the environment reach most episodes; restoring the agent's own state would have sufficed in 35 of 95 runs. A text scan of the raw corpus also shows that 45% of the hand-crafted Who&When failures ended with a provider content-filter crash after which the harness emitted a final answer no agent produced, a failure class that neither symptom taxonomies nor responsible-agent labels represent. Protocol, records and scripts are included.

papers.title: Polarized Equatorial Emission around Kerr Black Holes with Synchronized Scalar Hair. II. Indirect images
papers.abstract: We investigate the intensity polarization properties of the indirect images of a geometrically and optically thin accretion disk around fully self-consistent models of Kerr black holes with synchronized scalar hair. The presence of a massive, self-gravitating scalar field can dramatically alter the lensing properties of the spacetime, resulting in morphologically complex indirect images. We show that for a representative high scalar charge model, this results in the presence of high order central ring-like images at low observer inclinations. These images are not exponentially demagnified, and their polarized intensity, relative to the direct images, is significant. We therefore conclude that the observational signature of strongly scalarized Kerr black holes may not be dominated solely by the $n=1$ image, as images with $n\geq2$ may also contribute significantly to the observed polarized emission, depending on the radial emissivity profile of the disk and the observer inclination.

papers.title: Splitting for Stability: a Modified Reward Scheme for Transaction-Fee-Only Regimes
papers.abstract: As Bitcoin's block subsidy declines over time, miner revenue will come to depend increasingly on transaction fees. In fee-dominated regimes, winner-take-all reward structures can create incentives for undercutting and fork-based mining strategies, leading to instability and reduced transaction throughput. To prevent this instability, we propose a reward-splitting mechanism in which the winning block producer receives an $α$-portion of the block reward, while the rest is distributed among other miners; this incentivizes mining on previous blocks with higher rewards, while preserving the incentive to produce blocks with high rewards. We evaluate the proposed reward structure through analysis and simulation. Our analysis derives a local profitability condition for one-step Function-Fork deviations, showing how the winner-side reward, loser-side subsidy, and honest hash power jointly determine whether undercutting is profitable. Simulations show parameter regions in which honest behavior dominates fork-based deviations. In the cases where forking becomes dominant, the learned strategy is the least aggressive variant studied. The analysis and simulations suggest that suitable reward-splitting parameters can reduce the honest participation needed to suppress aggressive forking strategies relative to the winner-take-all structure studied in prior work. Finally, we show that the modified reward scheme does not appear to worsen selfish mining incentives. Together, these results suggest that reward redistribution can mitigate fee-driven fork incentives without introducing stronger selfish mining incentives, providing a possible direction for incentive design in fee-era proof-of-work systems.

papers.title: Curie's Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols
papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.

papers.title: Using Proof Dependencies to Manage Verification Projects
papers.abstract: Verification technology now scales to sizable projects, but techniques for managing such projects fall short. There are no effective ways to assess the progress made so far and to determine which verification tasks to perform next. A key issue is that the successful run of a verification tool provides little indication about what has actually been achieved. The guarantees provided depend on the specifications of the verified code as well as any unverified assumptions made in the proofs, e.g., about the behavior of unverified libraries. Manual inspection of specifications and assumptions to determine progress is error-prone and prohibitively expensive. In this paper, we present automated techniques to assess and guide verification projects. All of these techniques employ an automatic proof dependency analysis that computes, for each proof obligation in a project, the specifications, statements, and assumptions that are needed to prove it. We show that this analysis enables effective proof audits by determining all assumptions a proof depends on. We also use it to determine which statements in a program are constrained by the provided specifications, which indicates how strong a specification is. Based on these two insights, we propose a novel progress metric for verification projects and show how to use it to guide verification projects to maximize progress. We implement our approach in the symbolic execution backend of Viper and lift it to the Go verifier Gobra. Our evaluation on real-world benchmarks, including a verified Internet router, shows that the dependency analysis is sound and sufficiently precise, that our progress metric accurately reflects the state of a verification project over time, and that our guidance outperforms standard bottom-up and top-down verification strategies.

papers.title: Domain-Routed Delta Optimization for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation assigns each sample a domain teacher but typically updates shared student parameters. We introduce Domain-Routed Delta Optimization (DRD-MOPD), which specifies which parameter components each domain's samples update. The student is the sum of a frozen base and trainable components initialized from expert-minus-base weights. All components participate in every forward pass; four update modes define the correspondence between sample domains and components, each with independent optimizer states. We analyze these update rules and measure retention of the original expert geometry through angles, projection coefficients, and energy. Prior work such as Open-MOPD distills directly from the base model; 97.02% of its released final checkpoint's increment energy lies outside the span of the original expert directions. In comparison, our Own checkpoint after 20 updates retains coefficients near one along each component's original direction and pairwise angles ranging from 88.04 to 92.41 degrees; its exported BF16 student's increment has 4.90% outside energy, versus 10.52% for the sum of saved FP32 components. The same checkpoint achieves a 32.72% macro score across six benchmarks, compared with 32.44% for its initial task-arithmetic merge. These measurements describe geometry and capability at the evaluated training stages and settings.

papers.title: Hermitian K-theory for stable $\infty$-categories IV: Karoubi-Grothendieck-Witt theory
papers.abstract: In analogy with the passage from connective to non-connective algebraic K-theory, Schlichting put forward the Karoubi-Grothendieck-Witt spectrum as an approximation to Grothendieck-Witt theory by a functor invariant under idempotent completion. In this paper, we extend his construction to the setting of Poincaré $\infty$-categories and characterise the resulting functor by the expected universal property. Our main result places these Karoubi-Grothendieck-Witt-spectra in an exact sequence involving the ultimately decorated L-spectrum and homotopy orbits of non-connective K-theory. This confirms a conjecture of Williams which had remained open even for rings in which $2$ is invertible, and allows us to deduce universal characterisations for ultimately decorated L-theory. We obtain these results by unifying the Bass-Heller-Swan and Ranicki-Shaneson splittings into a general decomposition theorem that yields, in particular, formulas for Grothendieck-Witt groups of Laurent polynomial rings. Finally, we construct multiplicative structures on both versions of our Grothendieck-Witt and L-functors and refine their universal properties to multiplicative ones. Along the way, we show that the original versions are even idempotent with respect to Day convolution.

papers.title: Detectability of Seyfert galaxies in point-source and stacking searches with a global network of neutrino telescopes
papers.abstract: Recent evidence for high-energy neutrino emission from NGC 1068 and other nearby Seyfert galaxies suggests that active galactic nuclei (AGNs) may constitute a class of astrophysical neutrino sources. Using a physically motivated neutrino emission model based on stochastic particle acceleration in magnetized AGN coronae, we investigate the detection prospects of X-ray-bright Seyfert galaxies with a detector network comprising IceCube, Baikal-GVD, KM3NeT/ARCA, and P-ONE. We find that the Circinus Galaxy is the most promising point-source target in the Southern sky and will be detected at the 5$σ$ level by 2038 at the latest, provided that the Seyfert population accounts for the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux up to 100 TeV and Circinus is at least as efficient a neutrino emitter as the average source in the population. Individual detections of other nearby Seyferts are expected to remain challenging, making stacking searches informed by X-ray observations the most promising approach for discovering them within the next decade. Our results demonstrate that joint analyses across multiple neutrino telescopes, together with future MeV gamma-ray observations, will be essential for establishing Seyfert galaxies as astrophysical neutrino sources and provide a means for testing the coronal origin of their neutrino emission.

papers.title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
papers.abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.

papers.title: Rethinking Evaluation for Video Capsule Endoscopy: Validation Protocol, Source-Video Diversity, and Cross-Dataset Shift
papers.abstract: Automated video capsule endoscopy (VCE) classification remains challenging due to severe class imbalance, limited source-video diversity, and variations in image appearance across datasets. Although deep learning models have demonstrated promising performance on established benchmarks, their reliability under different validation protocols and external dataset shift remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we introduce DMSNet, a deformable adaptive multi-scale edge-guided attention network integrating adaptive multi-scale feature fusion, deformable lesion refinement, edge-guided attention, and sparse feature selection. We benchmark DMSNet against 18 representative convolutional, transformer-based, and pretrained vision architectures on Kvasir-Capsule under random frame-level and source-video-disjoint validation protocols. We further identify source-video overlap between the original training and test splits and evaluate model performance on both the complete test set and a source-video-disjoint subset. Under random frame-level validation, DMSNet achieves an MCC of 0.442 $\pm$ 0.020 on complete test set and 0.456 $\pm$ 0.037 on the source-video-disjoint subset. On the external CV2024 dataset, ConvNeXt-Tiny achieves the highest MCC of 0.207, while performance degrades substantially across architectures relative to in-domain evaluation. We further investigate source-video diversity using a per-class cap of 200 training frames. With the total training-set size held fixed, increasing the maximum source-video coverage from four to eight improves MCC for 17 of 19 evaluated architectures. Overall, these findings demonstrate that model rankings and classification performance depend substantially on evaluation protocol, training-source diversity, and cross-dataset shift, emphasizing the need for source-aware validation and rigorous external evaluation of VCE classification systems.

papers.title: Stabilization of the zero forcing number of generalized Petersen graphs
papers.abstract: We show that the zero forcing number of the generalized Petersen graph $P(n,k)$ is $2k+2$ whenever $n\ge 2k^2+k+1$. We prove this by showing that the zero forcing number of the infinite generalized Petersen graph $P(\infty,k)$ is $2k+2$ and bounding the width of the closure of every set of at most $2k+1$ vertices. This bound gives a threshold on $n$ beyond which the projection of such a closure onto $P(n,k)$ does not wrap around. Combined with an exhaustive computer search for smaller $n$, we determine the zero forcing number of every $P(n,k)$ for $k\le 5$.

papers.title: GigaEdge Spench: An SDK for Practical Streaming Speech Enhancement
papers.abstract: We present GigaEdge Spench, an open-source SDK for streaming speech enhancement on CPU servers, mobile devices, and in browsers. Applications can build enhancement channels from neural denoising, normalization and dynamics blocks, sample-rate conversion, and acoustic echo cancellation where supported. These stages can be combined, while normalization can also run without a neural model. The release includes an 8 kHz INT8 denoiser and discriminative and hybrid 48 kHz FP32 models. A shared C++ core supports ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite through native interfaces, Android and iOS SDKs, and WebAssembly integration. Independent stream contexts share model resources, and consecutive frames from one stream can be processed in a single inference call. We evaluate the released models on EARS-WHAM v2 and compare their quality and processing costs with RNNoise and DPDFNet2. All tested native and Web configurations process files faster than real time, although larger chunks require more time to collect input. We also measure how many streams a shared model can process on a CPU. Our contribution is a configurable deployment system and an experimental study of how model choice, chunk size, and execution environment affect its use. All reported SDK timing uses ONNX Runtime. Index Terms: speech enhancement, streaming inference, cross-platform deployment, temporal frame grouping, computational efficiency

papers.title: Molecular Gas Optics Using Vibrational Population Density Refraction
papers.abstract: Gas optics holds promise for development of advanced optical elements with 2-3 orders of magnitude higher damage threshold than any solid-state optics. Here, we demonstrate a new concept for refracting the laser beam using vibrationally excited molecules as gas optics instead of traditional control of thermodynamic gas temperature. The transient, vibrational population density grating is formed in a CO2 gas by interfering two mid-IR lasers to imprint spatial modulation in the linear refractive index (Delta n0 >=2x10-5) of the neutral gas via enhancement of the molecular polarizability. It is increased by pumping the asymmetric stretching mode of CO2 at optimal wavelengths to resonantly produce a highly nonequilibrium state that increases the effective vibrational mode temperature to greater than 2000 K in a room temperature gas. The measured beam steering efficiency of such a volume gas grating exceeds 90% that makes this approach a candidate for producing other large-aperture, high-throughput molecular optics elements, with expected damage thresholds 0.5-1 kJ/cm2, much-needed for future ultrahigh-power lasers.

papers.title: FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code can resolve real-world repository issues, but their iterative interaction loop can be expensive. Existing approaches reduce this cost primarily by limiting, compressing, or selectively avoiding information and actions within the repair process. We investigate a complementary question: Can an agent reason about a repair at an abstract program level, rather than repeatedly operating over raw source code, to reduce both the exploration needed to identify a repair and the repeated checking needed to verify it afterward? We present FlowPlan, an abstraction-guided repair approach that structures localization, planning, and verification around per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs. The agent first localizes the candidate fault location on the program abstraction and expresses the intended repair as explicit graph deltas before modifying the concrete source. After the edit, FlowPlan reconstructs the same abstraction and compares the observed structural change with the planned one. Then, a verification checks the complete repair before termination. Across all six benchmark-model settings, FlowPlan does not significantly change resolution rate relative to the vanilla agent while reducing token consumption in every setting, significantly in five of six settings. With Claude Haiku 4.5, it uses only 0.46-0.47x the baseline tokens on SWE-bench Pro, 0.32-0.35x on SWE-bench Verified, and 0.68-0.74x on SecBench; with Sonnet 5, it uses 0.72-0.76x, 0.73-0.74x, and 0.92-0.94x, respectively. Overall, FlowPlan achieves the largest token reduction among the compared methods in three of the six settings and ties the strongest compared method in a fourth. Trajectory analysis shows that FlowPlan saves tokens by replacing much of the costly post-edit re-reading and testing with explicit verification and reducing per-call context.

papers.title: A decomposition theorem for minimal W-algebras of type A
papers.abstract: To any simple Lie algebra, one can associate a minimal affine W-algebra. It is a vertex algebra which is obtained from the universal affine vertex algebra by a chiral Hamiltonian reduction procedure. This reduction is determined by data coming from the minimal nilpotent orbit. It is a chiral quantisation of the Slodowy slice associated to this minimal orbit. In this paper, when the simple Lie algebra is of type A, we prove that the minimal W-algebra is isomorphic to a commutant subalgebra in a localisation of the universal affine vertex algebra. Then, we establish a decomposition theorem à la Losev: the localised universal affine vertex algebra decomposes as the tensor product of the minimal affine W-algebra and another vertex subalgebra. As a direct corollary, we retrieve the celebrated result of inverse Hamiltonian reduction for the minimal W-algebra. We also prove an analogue of this result for the corresponding finite W-algebra. In both cases, our approach relies on the geometry of the associated Slodowy slice.

papers.title: STAR: Semantic-Criticality Tiered Allocation of Radio Resources via Zero-Shot Learning
papers.abstract: In remote inference, edge devices transmit high-resolution images over wireless links to a receiver, where an artificial intelligence (AI) model answers task-specific questions about these images to enable reliable decisions. These answers are often determined by a small set of task-causal pixels, such as those of text, whose corruption changes the answer, so these pixels must be delivered with high fidelity. Conventional transmission protects every pixel equally, so it either consumes many resource elements (REs) or corrupts these regions at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). To overcome these limitations, in this paper, a zero-shot, domain-agnostic framework, termed semantic-criticality tiered allocation of resources (STAR), is proposed. In particular, a per-pixel semantic-criticality indicator (SCI) is derived from the attention of a frozen vision-language model, so new tasks and domains are handled by changing only the prompt, without retraining. The resulting task causality-aware resource allocation problem over protection tiers is solved exactly by a threshold rule on the SCI, realized by a coded tier for the task-causal pixels and an uncoded, downsampled base layer for the full image. Simulations over a 5G New Radio link demonstrate that STAR attains a semantic accuracy of at least 0.98 for $E_s/N_0 \geq -4$ dB and, at comparable semantic reliability, reduces the REs of robust coded transmission by 59.5% and 91.5% on factory- and vehicle-monitoring datasets, respectively, the latter without any change to the models. Although a deep joint source-channel coding baseline uses fewer REs at comparable semantic accuracy, it must be retrained with labeled data for every new task or domain.

papers.title: Understanding Computing Instructors' Perceptions of Student Sense of Belonging
papers.abstract: Students' sense of belonging has been described as a feeling of community acceptance, respect, inclusion, and membership. In computing, student belonging is shaped by psychological, social, academic, and environmental factors, including their relationships with instructors. However, despite prior work emphasizing instructors' influence on student belonging, limited research has examined how computing instructors perceive, understand, and attempt to support belonging. Through nine semi-structured qualitative interviews with introductory computing instructors at large public universities in the United States, we investigated how instructors define, measure, and conceptualize belonging; what interventions they use to support student belonging; and what barriers limit the efficacy of these interventions. Our findings show that instructors defined belonging through value and identity representation, self-efficacy, and community; relied on surveys, observations, and student performance to measure belonging; saw belonging to be influenced by prior experience, major, student and institutional culture, and representation; implemented student-oriented interventions and designed courses around belonging; and identified multi-level challenges to supporting belonging. These results highlight opportunities to design belonging interventions that attend to both prior work and instructor conceptualizations, while also considering tensions in utilizing teaching assistants, balancing students' expectations, and adapting to broader societal trends affecting belonging.

papers.title: NCP: Verifier-Guided Optimization of Weight-Space Control Policies
papers.abstract: We present the Neural Control Plane (NCP), a closed-loop system that observes language-model execution, synthesizes candidate weight-space intervention rules, evaluates them, and maintains a versioned table of admitted policies. NCP separates a pretrained model's inference data plane from the control policy that selects temporary parameter interventions. W-ISA supplies transactional execution and parameter restoration; NCP supplies telemetry, candidate synthesis, admission criteria, priorities, and rule lifetime management. The optimization state consists of active rules and an archive of evaluated candidates, while base-model parameters are restored after each request. In a local SmolLM-135M-Instruct experiment, NCP generated three candidates from development telemetry and evaluated them on separate task examples and a 4,095-target WikiText-2 slice. One projection reduced validation token repetition from 0.4133 to 0.2191, with a perplexity change of -0.0574%. All candidates produced zero newly correct exact answers, so the configured admission gate archived all three and retained the original active policy. Fresh-process repetition and saved-table resumption reproduced the measured outcomes. NCP provides an executable framework for studying recursive self-improvement at the control-policy level through explicit synthesis, verification, and state transitions.

papers.title: Neutron Scattering studies of the density dependence of One-dimensional Quantum Fluids
papers.abstract: In previous work, we demonstrated that $^4$He confined within a templated porous material preplated with a noble gas to enhance dimensional reduction exhibits one-dimensional behavior. Neutron scattering revealed that the excitations in confined $^4$He are qualitatively distinct from those in two- and three-dimensional superfluid helium, aligning with quantum Monte Carlo calculations. These simulations suggest that three solid layers form, with a one-dimensional liquid located at the center of the pore. Here, we present neutron scattering results as the filling fraction of the one-dimensional core is varied. We observe that the one-dimensional liquid always forms with a fixed density, even as the pore filling increases. We posit that this is due to the growth of the one dimensional extent of the liquid as the filling is increased, but its density remains unchanged.

papers.title: The Alpha Clustering Model of the EMC Effect
papers.abstract: For more than forty years, the EMC effect, the observation that nuclear structure functions in deep-inelastic scattering appear to be modified relative to the free-nucleon expectation, has resisted a consensus microscopic explanation. In this letter, we argue that the strength and $A$ dependence of the EMC effect may be governed by the phenomena of $α$ clustering in nuclei and responsible for a majority of the partonic modification associated with the EMC Effect. We motivate the alpha clustering model of the EMC effect (ACME), and with a data driven approach, we demonstrate how such a model can reproduce the existing deep inelastic scattering data on nuclei. We make predictions for other nuclei such as $^{16}$O, $^{20}$Ne, and $^{48}$Ca and explore its consequences for a spin-dependent EMC effect and global analysis of nuclear parton distributions.

papers.title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides a testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.

papers.title: W-ISA: Transactional Execution of Weight-Space Intervention Programs
papers.abstract: We present W-ISA, a software instruction set and transactional runtime for executing weight-space intervention programs on pretrained language models. Shape-checked instructions express parameter updates, projections, ablations, and rank-one transformations. The runtime applies these programs within request-scoped execution contexts and restores saved parameters after completion or interruption. Activation-based match-action rules connect measured model states to intervention selection. We evaluate restoration and replay on SmolLM-135M-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and compare materialized rank-one updates with equivalent PyTorch hooks on the latter. In 45 timed requests, both intervention implementations produce identical greedy sequences at 32, 128, and 512 tokens; their maximum prompt-logit difference is 0.000184. On the complete WikiText-2 raw test split, the combined SmolLM attention-head ablation and MLP projection changes perplexity from 22.2353 to 22.3188, a relative increase of 0.3754%. W-ISA separates intervention specification, execution, and measurement, making parameter-level experiments reproducible and composable.

papers.title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach
papers.abstract: In this work, we develop an efficient Gauss-Newton optimization approach for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs). The key ingredient is the overlapping domain decomposition architecture of FBPINNs, which localizes the influence of each subnetwork and induces block sparsity in both the residual Jacobian and the corresponding Gauss-Newton matrix. We characterize this structure and exploit it through sparse automatic differentiation, using graph coloring to partition structurally orthogonal Jacobian columns or rows. This reduces differentiation costs and memory requirements while preserving all structurally nonzero derivative information. The resulting compressed Jacobian representations allow us to assemble the Gauss-Newton system directly in block-sparse form, enabling the use of sparse direct solvers and preconditioned iterative methods. In this way, the otherwise expensive second-order optimization problem is reduced to scalable sparse linear algebra. We demonstrate the approach on multiscale PDEs, where accurate approximation requires rich neural network parametrizations and large numbers of collocation points. Numerical experiments show that our block-sparse Gauss-Newton method attains high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines while remaining computationally tractable for large problem sizes.

papers.title: Dynamic investment and coordination in teams: Theory and experimental evidence
papers.abstract: Teamwork requires more than the general skills that team members bring. In successful teams, members invest in team-specific skill or capital that accumulates within the team and raises the return to coordinated production. We provide the first systematic analysis of dynamic investment in such team skill. Adopting a dynamic game approach, we develop a novel theoretical framework where investment in team skill creates persistent benefits but is risky because the benefits depend on successful team coordination. We then take this framework to the laboratory to study empirically the factors that influence dynamic investment in team skill. We find underinvestment compared to the efficient benchmark. However, investment responds strongly to incentives, in line with specific theory-predicted patterns. Pre-registered traits (theory of mind and propensity to coordinate) predict investment and team-level efficiency. We conclude that careful design of team incentives and selection of team members can facilitate the development of team skill.

papers.title: Incorporating World Models in Decision Making for Next Best View Selection in Active Sensing
papers.abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. Pretrained world models can guide this choice, but a predicted surface may not produce valid depth measurements under the operating conditions of the deployed sensor. We present a deployment adaptation methodology for next-best-view selection that learns a sensor-return adapter from limited local calibration data while keeping the pretrained predictor fixed. The adapter estimates measurement dropout over each predicted surface, allowing the selection method to favor views likely to fill gaps in the measured reconstruction. In a real-robot experiment with a structured-light sensor, the adapted method achieves higher measured surface coverage with 60% fewer captures than nominal selection. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.

papers.title: Continuous Horizon Forecasting
papers.abstract: Multi-horizon forecasting has been dominated by discrete forecast strategies that treat model outputs as fixed-vectors or recurrently create them. In this paper, we introduce the Continuous Horizon (CH) strategy that generalizes upon recursive, direct, and multi-step strategies by redefining forecasts as a continuous operator and the forecast horizon as a query variable rather than an index. We present the theoretical foundations for the CH strategy, a Universal Operator Approximation Theorem, and a continuous-horizon bias-variance decomposition that formally proves the estimation variance improvements of CH over the discrete strategies. We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.

papers.title: Latent Barrier Steering: Hierarchical Safety for Generative Planning
papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.

papers.title: Unilluminable rooms: minimal examples, classifications and exceptions
papers.abstract: A room with mirrored walls can contain two points that are mutually invisible: no light ray from one reaches the other. Tokarsky built the first polygonal examples by tiling a room with reflected copies of a triangle and making every tile vertex of certain kinds a corner of the room. We study the smallest rooms of this kind, which we call lattice rooms. Their interior tile vertices of the remaining kind, the sources, are invisible and pairwise mutually invisible. On the tiling by isosceles right triangles, a hole-free lattice room with a source has at least 12 sides, attained only by the pinwheel. On the square tiling the least number is 16, again attained by one room. A hole-free lattice room with two sources has at least 24 sides on the first tiling and 34 on the square tiling. Up to congruence there are 12 such rooms with 24 sides, 89 with 25 sides and 14 with 34 sides. One absorbing post, one partition, or one hole that touches the outer boundary at one point lowers the least number of sides for two sources to 18, 20 and 22 (21 if sides are counted as maximal straight segments). Two and three posts give 17 and 16 sides, and a hole that does not touch the outer boundary gives 26. We list all smallest rooms. Rooms assembled from n modules have exactly 12n sides and n sources, and a hole-free lattice room with three or more sources has at least 36 sides. We also give rooms in which some tile vertices need not be corners: 15 types of 27-sided rooms on the tiling by triangles with angles 30, 60 and 90 degrees, which are smallest in their class, a nonagon with three mutually invisible corners, and a 42-sided room in which a rotation through 180 degrees takes the place of a corner. In a ring of three trapezoids a light ray returns to a corner that is invisible in one trapezoid. Several classifications rely on exhaustive computer searches made finite by the bounds proved here.

papers.title: Intermediate-redshift slow rotators as the progenitors of the most massive galaxies at z $\sim$ 0
papers.abstract: We study the resolved stellar kinematics and star formation histories, and their dependence on the environment, in a sample of 218 intermediate redshift (0.1 < z < 1) galaxies located in the CANDELS and COSMOS fields, observed with VLT/MUSE. The sample covers galaxies with stellar masses ranging M_star ~10^8 - 10^12 M_sun, including both star-forming and quiescent systems. For 113 galaxies, found in dense environments of galaxy groups, we derive the spin parameter ($λ_{R}$), while for the rest of the sample, we use data from previous papers in this series. Given that the surveys used in this work are flux-limited, the $λ_{R}$ distribution of our full sample lacks the bimodality observed in the local Universe, but the subsample of galaxies at z < 0.6 resembles the galaxy population in the nearby Universe, in terms of mass, sizes, and stellar population properties, more than galaxies at z > 0.6. We classified the galaxies into fast and slow rotators, finding that ~8% (17/218) of the galaxies are slow-rotating. The fraction of slow rotators does not change significantly down to z = 0, but we find that in the z ~ 0 sample, the spin parameter is, on average, higher than at higher redshifts. In our subsample at z > 0.6, we observed evidence for the existence of the kinematic morphology-density relation. The slow rotators in our sample mostly assemble their stellar mass in one or two main episodes of formation, and they finished assembling their mass via star formation by redshift of z $\sim$ 1. It is however, not clear if the loss of angular momentum can be associated with the last star formation episode. Based on their location in the mass - size diagram, the intermediate-redshift galaxies are consistent with being the progenitors of the most massive slow rotators observed at z~0, where the subsequent growth is facilitated through gas-poor (dry) mergers.

papers.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
papers.abstract: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.

papers.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement across Seven Open Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Across 94k ShareGPT conversations, 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and the task cost of this stripping remains unmeasured. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, 794 tasks, and the official checker. The same deletion spans -4.4 to +51.3 points with both ends excluding zero, and for the one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property. The reading follows the model itself and stays constant across deployments, and a retrained or re-released model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing and aggregation as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

papers.title: AlphaHits: Full-Event Tracking and Reconstruction Towards a Hit-Level Foundation Model
papers.abstract: We introduce AlphaHits, a Transformer-based approach towards hit-level foundation models for LHC physics, building on the TrackFormer and HiggsFormer architectures. AlphaHits operates directly on detector hits and demonstrates scalable full-event charged-particle reconstruction and multi-task event reconstruction and classification from low-level detector information. AlphaHits-TrackFormer reconstructs the full charged-particle content of complete TrackML events without imposing a transverse-momentum selection on the target tracks. It processes both pixel and strip hits in events containing up to $1.5\times10^5$ hits under HL-LHC-like pileup conditions and assigns hits to individual reconstructed trajectories across its kinematic range. This includes the challenging low-$p_T$ population down to approximately $150\,\mathrm{MeV}$ in TrackML samples. It achieves a TrackML score of 0.959 over all reconstructable tracks, representing, to our knowledge, the highest reported TrackML score for full-detector, inclusive charged-particle reconstruction. Building on the TrackFormer architecture, AlphaHits is pretrained on charged-particle tracking and fine-tuned for multi-task reconstruction and classification. From a shared hit-level representation, it predicts tracks, jets, jet flavour, and event-level observables. AlphaHits achieves an AUC of 0.944 for Higgs event classification, with performance comparable to a Particle Transformer (ParT) baseline using fully reconstructed inputs. It also achieves performance comparable to Delphes-based baselines for jet reconstruction, jet flavour classification, and missing transverse momentum regression. These results highlight the potential for scalable full-event tracking and multi-task learning directly from detector hits, representing a promising step towards transferable hit-level representations and general-purpose foundation models for LHC physics.

papers.title: Exceptional points in non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion: From coefficient dynamics to state signatures
papers.abstract: An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form $O$ operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.

papers.title: Optimality Guarantees for Minimum Variance Subset Selection via Semidefinite Programming
papers.abstract: Given a set of data points in Euclidean space and a prescribed cardinality $k$, the minimum variance $k$-subset problem asks for $k$ points minimizing their average squared distance from their centroid. We develop a semidefinite programming (SDP) framework for exact recovery and global optimization. First, we show that the natural SDP relaxation fails Slater's condition. Identifying the proper face containing its feasible region yields an equivalent, lower-dimensional, strictly feasible formulation that enjoys strong duality. A primal--dual characterization of optimality then gives geometric necessary and sufficient conditions under which the SDP relaxation is guaranteed to be tight.
